## Why a lighthouse lens is made of rings

A lighthouse has to throw a beam many miles. A single glass lens big enough to do that would be as thick as a person is tall, far too heavy to turn and nearly opaque at the edges. The Fresnel lens solves the problem with a simple idea: most of a lens's glass does nothing but carry the curve along.

Augustin Fresnel noticed that bending light depends on the angle of the surface, not on how much glass lies behind it. So he cut away the bulk and kept only the curved faces, stepping them down in rings. The result bends light the same way at a fraction of the weight.
> "Light does not care how thick the glass is. It cares about the angle it meets."
Here is the idea in three steps:

- Start with a thick convex lens that focuses light at a point.
- Remove the glass inside each zone, keeping only the surface angle.
- Stack the zones as concentric rings, brightest at the centre.
![A lens, drawn here as a ring of gold on black](http://localhost:5733/icon-512x512.png)

The larger the order, the longer the focal length and the farther the beam reaches. A first order lens could be seen from about twenty nautical miles on a clear night.
## What to take from it

Thick is not the same as strong. When part of a design only carries something along, you can often remove it and keep the shape that matters. Fresnel did this with glass; the same move shows up in bridges, in antennas and in how a good essay cuts a paragraph that only repeats the one before it.
